look_here_first: TOBOSA / Hilaria mutica (also Pleuraphis mutica): FIRST photograph the TRUE inner 0.5–2 mm, torn-edged membranous ligule at the blade–sheath junction; note stiff 2–4 mm blades and short hairs on the blade just BEHIND the ligule. SECOND inspect attached dense 4–8 cm head of repeated 5–8 mm three-spikelet groups and, where possible, detached mature fascicles. Archived photographs prove whole flowering clusters and gross head structure, NOT the individual fertile central versus lateral staminate spikelets. Only LATER evaluate the short thick underground rhizomes to confirm against curlymesquite's surface stolons. Do not confuse the false ligule appearance of leaf hairs with the true membrane.

best_field_traits: Perennial, often coarse sod/bunch grass with short thick SCALY underground rhizomes and NO aboveground spreading stolons.
Culms commonly ~30–70 cm tall in regional treatment; stout wiry rigid aspect, often ash gray in drought.
Most leaves basal, stiff and narrow (often ~2–5 mm in Hill Country flora), sometimes rolling inward in dry conditions; nodes can be pubescent.
True membranous ligule about 1–2 mm long, often torn/lacerate; base of blade may have a few long hairs that are NOT the ligule.
Flowering axis a single compact spike-like head, often roughly 7–8 cm, bearing ~8–25 tightly placed fascicles (groups of three spikelets) with broad/modified hairy glumes.
Fascicles disarticulate as an entire group, leaving behind a characteristic zigzag rachis.
Alternate name Pleuraphis mutica in some regional sources; authoritative ITIS/GRIN and POWO treat Hilaria mutica as the accepted concept.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Full 30–70 cm perennial patch with woody/tough stems visible in habitat.
Exposed short thick scaly RHIZOME physically attached to tuft, with mm ruler; restore soil after photo.
Blade and collar macro with true 1–2 mm tattered membranous ligule.
Whole compact spikelike head showing groups of THREE spikelets.
One intact three-spikelet fascicle plus empty zigzag rachis with 5-mm ruler.
crew_field_check: Trace stems to base: does this grass use aboveground rooted stolons or buried scaly rhizomes?
Check collar true ligule under magnification, then one intact three-spikelet fascicle.
Never call a species from zigzag rachis or dry color alone.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Curlymesquite (H. belangeri) forms a SHORT stoloniferous turf with aboveground runners and hairy rooting nodes, often 10–30 cm tall, whereas tobosa is generally taller/coarser and has BELOWGROUND thick scaly rhizomes, without stolons. Both can display triads of spikelets and residual zigzag axes. Vine mesquite (Hopia obtusa) has VERY LONG surface stolons with swollen hairy nodes rather than the tough short scaly tobosa rhizomes, and does not share tobosa's exact tightly triad-grouped spikelet structure.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · FIND THE TRUE LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.details: At the inner blade–sheath junction, inspect the torn-looking (lacerate) membranous ligule, about 0.5–2 mm long in Flora of North America; Kew GrassBase describes about 1 mm. Blades are commonly 2–4 mm wide, stiff and rough. Hairs behind the ligule are NOT the free ligule edge. An opened collar with millimeter scale is needed.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED COLLAR MEASUREMENT; PIXEL PROOF MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · COUNT THE THREE-SPIKELET GROUPS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Dense terminal 4–8 cm head; triads 5–8 mm
field_id_short_tiles.details: The compact terminal spikelike panicle is commonly 4–8 cm long and consists of repeated 5–8 mm fascicles. Each group carries ONE central fertile spikelet and TWO lateral predominantly staminate spikelets. These are THREE distinct spikelets, not three florets inside one spikelet. Detached groups may leave a zigzag axis shared with curlymesquite.
field_id_short_tiles.status: HEAD PHOTO AVAILABLE; CALIBRATED FASCICLE MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE CENTRAL FERTILE SPIKELET
field_id_short_tiles.short: Central spikelet about 6–8 mm; lobed glumes
field_id_short_tiles.details: Kew GrassBase describes the central fertile spikelet about 6–8 mm long, containing one bisexual fertile floret. Its glumes have divergent dorsal awns and lobed/fringed apices; the central lemma extends beyond the glumes and is bilobed, often mucronate. A Kew treatment describes a short ~1-mm lemma awn from the sinus; FNA emphasizes mucronate lemmas. Keep the literature distinction and do not label glume awns as lemma awns.
field_id_short_tiles.status: LITERATURE KEY; CENTRAL BRActs NOT DISSECTED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · INSPECT THE TWO LATERAL SPIKELETS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Male companions often 4–8 mm; glumes lobed
field_id_short_tiles.details: Two lateral male/staminate companion spikelets flank the central fertile one. Kew describes them as approximately 4–8 mm long, with 1–2 (occasionally more) staminate florets; FNA describes glumes as papery, lobed and fringed, with dorsal awns not exceeding the tips. Expose the lateral glumes and lemmas separately at 1-mm scale before drawing arrows; a whole fascicle photograph cannot prove bract insertion.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · TOBOSA OR CURLYMESQUITE?
field_id_short_tiles.short: Belowground scaly rhizome versus aboveground runner
field_id_short_tiles.details: Curlymesquite (H. belangeri) forms short turf with thin wiry ABOVEGROUND stolons rooting at hairy nodes; tobosa spreads by SHORT THICK SCALY UNDERGROUND rhizomes and is generally taller/coarser. Both bear three-spikelet fascicles and may leave zigzag axes. Vine mesquite has long aboveground runners with swollen nodes but lacks the same triad architecture. Do not use dry gray color or a solitary seedhead as species proof. Pleuraphis mutica is an alternative genus placement, not a second species.
field_id_short_tiles.status: LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES EXPLAINED; MATCHED ROOTS NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · OPTIONAL BELOWGROUND CONFIRMATION
field_id_short_tiles.short: Coarse perennial: expose the short scaly rhizome
field_id_short_tiles.details: Tobosa is a perennial forming tough coarse patches, with culms often 30–60 cm in Flora of North America. The decisive growth clue is a SHORT THICK SCALY RHIZOME BELOW SOIL attached to the culm, not an aboveground rooting stolon. The current photographs do not show a connected excavated rhizome; do not arrow a basal sheath as one.
